rawContent:
Tweet by @Cdempsey44 (Connor Dempsey)
Author bio: stablecoins @raincards
Text: Hey Omid, author here. Thanks for reading the piece and for the feedback. 

A few things we think you're missing:

On interchange - there would be little incentive for issuers to issue cards if they couldn't monetize it. Yes they work where interchange is capped, but capped does not mean zero. Capped interchange just means less rewards, as you note. In places with capped interchange you also tend to see higher annual fees to compensate.

On settlement - you're right that the largest banks don't have this problem. But our post is not addressing the problems of JPMorgan. The problems we describe are very real for small and mid-sized banks and fintechs. And the rails you point to (same-day ACH, RTP, FedNow) are US systems. Much of the market issuing cards sits outside the US with no access to them at all. As a few people have already pointed out in your replies.

On cross-border - Visa settles in about 25 currencies and the Colombian peso is not one of them, so the example stands. The problems of interfacing with the correspondent banking system are real for programs in LatAm and elsewhere looking to serve a broader audience.

On where this ends up, we agree: stablecoin cards are a bridge step to mass adoption of stablecoins, which will also have merchants accepting stablecoins directly. It is hard to see how this will be done in a pure peer-to-peer manner, as people will still want chargebacks and fraud disputes.

But we will see networks evolve, or new networks emerge that operate solely in stablecoins.
